claims.text: Local chemical heterogeneity governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
A random distribution of different atomic species produces spatial variations in bond strength.
A random distribution of different atomic species produces local lattice strain.
Variations in bond strength and lattice strain broaden the onset of surface premelting.
Chemical heterogeneity depresses the effective melting point relative to monometallic or simpler-alloy nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles can be treated as solid, single-phase particles.
The initial particles have a well-mixed, near-random elemental distribution in an fcc or comparable lattice.
The proposed test heats and subsequently cools the particles across the premelting and melting regimes under inert conditions while monitoring phase evolution in situ.
Surface-energy effects dominate the thermal behavior of particles in the proposed 5–50 nm size range.
Differences in atomic size and electronegativity create weakly bonded regions at the nanoparticle surface.
High configurational entropy gives rise to different local atomic neighborhoods within a single nanoparticle.
Regions with weaker interactions or greater local strain undergo surface disorder at lower temperatures.
Sequential disordering of chemically distinct regions produces a gradual rather than sharp melting transition.
Relative to size- and structure-matched monometallic or binary controls, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a broader, lower-temperature premelting interval.
Surface amorphization or disorder will occur well before complete melting of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particle core.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to bulk material or to nanoparticles with substantial phase segregation or nonuniform elemental distributions.
The quantitative relationship between local compositional fluctuations and melting-point depression is not established.
Particle size and defect density may modify the proposed relationship between chemical heterogeneity and thermal response.
Thermal behavior indistinguishable from matched monometallic or binary controls would falsify the predicted heterogeneity-induced alteration.
